passage: The student council at their Addis Ababa school had one day to make posters to save the old vegetable garden, which the principal wanted to pave for parking. Hana stayed up with markers and brought her slogan in huge green letters: GROW IT OR LOSE IT. Her classmates loved it. Abebe punched the air. "That's it. That's us." But at break Mr Tesfaye stopped in front of the poster and frowned. "Is this a threat? Lose what? Your respect for the principal?" Hana's face fell. She had only meant losing the garden. Abebe read it again, slowly, as if he were a teacher. "He's not wrong. It does sound like a warning." They stood there for five minutes, trying words. Finally Hana crossed out the last three and wrote underneath, smaller: GROW IT. SHARE IT. EAT IT. Mr Tesfaye came by later and laughed. "That one I would sign."

qa.q: What did Hana's first slogan say?
qa.a: It said GROW IT OR LOSE IT in huge green letters.

qa.q: What was Hana feeling when Mr Tesfaye asked 'Is this a threat?'
qa.a: Hana felt disappointed and a bit hurt, her face falling, since she only meant losing the garden; she may also have been surprised that four words could be read so differently.

qa.q: How did Hana and Abebe fix the slogan?
qa.a: They reread it the way a teacher might, tried words for five minutes and changed it to GROW IT. SHARE IT. EAT IT., which kept the energy but lost the warning.

qa.q: Why might Mr Tesfaye react differently from Hana's classmates?
qa.a: The classmates heard team spirit, while Mr Tesfaye heard a possible warning to the principal; the same short words fit both readings.

grounding: It shows a teenager's campaign slogan compressing attitude into a few words and being read one way by peers and another way by a teacher.

passage:
Hi Mehak,
I'm writing this properly because my text last night came out all wrong. When you said you couldn't come to the birthday dinner because of your cousin's engagement, I wrote "wow thanks for nothing". In my head I said it in the voice of our old maths teacher, the dramatic one, and I was grinning. On your screen it was just four cold words. You replied "ok sorry" and then nothing, and I realised you thought I was actually angry. I wasn't. I was disappointed for about five seconds, then happy that you'll be at an engagement with the famous dancing uncle. Next time I'll add a 😜 or just call you when it matters. Can I ring you after school today? I'm saving you a piece of cake either way, the corner one with extra icing.
Uday

qa.q: What did Uday text when Mehak couldn't come?
qa.a: Uday texted "wow thanks for nothing".

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when typing the text?
qa.a: Uday was only briefly disappointed and mostly playful, grinning at the dramatic teacher voice; the letter shows worry afterwards about having hurt Mehak.

qa.q: What could Uday do to avoid this next time?
qa.a: Add an emoji or a clarifying line to show the joke, or call when something matters, since the voice and the grin never reach the screen. 🙂

qa.q: What was 'ok sorry' likely to mean from Mehak's side?
qa.a: Mehak most likely read the four words as real anger and felt hurt or guilty, answering with a short apology and went quiet.

grounding: It shows a joking message reading as rude without face and voice, and a clarifying letter and a call being used to repair it.

passage:
Choir supervisor's note, Wednesday
Gargi was quiet all through warm-ups today, which is unusual. At break she showed me the group chat: on Sunday she had posted a recording of her solo, and in three days it had one reaction, a thumbs-up from Joseph. "Everyone listened and nobody liked it," she said, voice tight. I told her reactions are small, quick things; lots of people read and move on, and a missing one isn't a verdict. She didn't look convinced. So I asked the group, casually, who had heard Gargi's recording. Eleven hands went up. Two said they had played it twice on the bus. Joseph said his thumbs-up meant "that high note, wow". Gargi laughed and covered her face. Afterwards I suggested to the group that if something moves us, a line of words is worth sending. I'll keep an eye on how Gargi is on Friday.

qa.q: How many reactions did Gargi's recording get in three days?
qa.a: It had one reaction, a thumbs-up from Joseph.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when she said 'nobody liked it'?
qa.a: Gargi felt hurt and discouraged, voice tight, reading the missing reactions as rejection; part of it may also have been nerves about the solo itself.

qa.q: What did the supervisor do that helped?
qa.a: The supervisor explained that reactions are lightweight, then checked with the group, which showed eleven people had listened, and encouraged sending words when something moves them.

qa.q: What did Joseph's thumbs-up mean to Joseph?
qa.a: To Joseph it meant 'that high note, wow', a quick sign of real admiration rather than a lukewarm one.

grounding: It shows reaction buttons as lightweight signals of support, and a teenager learning that a missing reaction does not mean rejection.

subtype: Memes and GIFs as shared language [Expressing]
passage: The wedding was in a village with one bar of signal, and Vidya was standing on a plastic chair on the terrace trying to catch it when the family group lit up. Chaitanya: "GOT IN!! Pune college, computer science!!" Vidya grinned and sent their old in-joke, a GIF of a dog howling at a departing train. Since they were ten, it had meant I'm proud of you and I'll miss you. Chaitanya replied at once with the same GIF. Ten seconds later Nani called, the line crackling. "Vidya? Why is the dog crying? Are you upset he's going? Are you jealous?" Vidya nearly laughed, then heard the real worry in Nani's voice. The call dropped. She had maybe one message before the signal vanished again. She typed fast: "Nani, the dog is our joke. It means very proud, will miss him. Not sad. Congrats Chaitu!! 🎉" It went through with one tick, then two.

qa.q: What does the dog GIF mean between Vidya and Chaitanya?
qa.a: It means I'm proud of you and I'll miss you.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when she heard Nani's worry?
qa.a: Vidya felt amused at first, then concerned and rushed, realising Nani was really worried and the signal might vanish; there is also fondness for the old joke.

qa.q: How did Vidya repair the confusion despite the poor signal?
qa.a: She sent one clear line in plain words explaining the joke and adding congratulations, so Nani could read the meaning without knowing the in-joke.

qa.q: How did the GIF look to Nani?
qa.a: To Nani a howling dog looked like real sadness or even jealousy, so she called, worried.

grounding: It shows a GIF carrying pride and belonging between two people who share the joke, while confusing an outsider, since context and audience shape its meaning.

passage: Everyone in their Stockholm class agreed Emeka had the best feed: a sunset from the ferry, a perfect cinnamon bun, basketball mid-air. Ulla scrolled it on the bus home and felt a small hard knot in her chest. Her own weekend had been laundry and a fight with her brother. On Monday she said, a bit sharply, "Must be nice, living in a postcard." Emeka laughed, then stopped. "That sunset? I took forty photos and posted one. I was only on the ferry because my dad's shift moved and I had to pick up my sister. I was freezing." Ulla blinked. Then Emeka added, "Also, I posted the one from the class trip where your eyes are half closed. Sorry, I didn't ask. Want me to take it down?" "Yes, please," Ulla said. He deleted it while she watched, and they picked a better one together, which he posted only after she nodded.

qa.q: How many sunset photos did Emeka take?
qa.a: Emeka took forty photos and posted one.

qa.q: What was Ulla feeling as she scrolled Emeka's feed on the bus?
qa.a: Ulla felt a hard knot of resentment and envy, comparing a weekend of laundry and a fight with postcard-like photos; tiredness may also have made the gap feel bigger.

qa.q: What did Emeka do well?
qa.a: Emeka was honest that the sunset was one shot of forty and told the real story, and asked before reposting Ulla's picture, posting only after she nodded.

qa.q: What was it like for Emeka to hear 'living in a postcard'?
qa.a: It probably stung a little, since the real day was freezing and full of chores, and it also reminded Emeka that he hadn't asked about Ulla's photo.

grounding: It shows a teenager curating photos to present a polished self, a peer's resentment at the comparison, and asking consent before sharing someone else's image.

Pradeep: good. and thank you. monday was going to be a mess for me

qa.q: Which day did Urmila offer to take instead?

qa.q: What was Urmila worried about on seeing 'okay.'?
qa.a: Urmila was worried that Pradeep was annoyed, since in Urmila's group a full stop feels like a door slam; it could just as well have been a habit, which it turned out to be.

qa.q: Why was asking directly the right move?
qa.a: Punctuation only suggests a mood and norms differ, so asking cleared up that the full stops were a letter-writing habit, not coldness.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see a full stop?
qa.a: For Pradeep a full stop is just normal punctuation, taught by Pradeep's dad; real annoyance would come as a whole paragraph.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading a full stop as cold and capitals and repeated letters as excitement, while learning such cues differ from person to person.

subtype: Drama and mime as emotional language [Expressing]
passage: In the community centre's drama workshop, the prompt was one word on a chit: loss. Devika had two minutes and no lines. She knelt centre stage, cupped her hands as if holding something small and warm, then slowly opened them and stared at the empty space. Her shoulders shook once. She tried to close her hands again around nothing. The room went so quiet you could hear the ceiling fan tick. When she stood and bowed, people clapped late, blinking. Afterwards Dilnaz caught her at the water cooler, eyes wide. "Devika, are you okay? Did someone... die?" Devika shook her head, a little embarrassed. "No. I thought about my grandmother's old parrot, a bit. Mostly I just imagined what empty hands would feel like." Dilnaz let out a breath. "It looked so real." "That's the point," said Ms Arora, passing with the chits. "But you were right to ask."

qa.q: What word was on the chit?
qa.a: The word on the chit was loss.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when Dilnaz asked if someone had died?
qa.a: Devika seemed a little embarrassed at being taken literally; she had drawn on a small real sadness about the parrot but was mostly imagining, so the mime was not a confession.

qa.q: Why was Ms Arora's comment helpful?
qa.a: It honoured the acting as real craft while saying that asking was right, so feelings can be explored safely on stage and friends can still check in.

qa.q: What was it like for Dilnaz to watch the mime?
qa.a: Dilnaz was moved and worried, eyes wide, because it looked so real that she feared something had happened to Devika.

grounding: It shows a teenager using mime to portray grief at a safe distance, and a peer learning that a powerful role is not a confession of real events.

passage: At the youth centre's open mic in Lyon, Leila gripped the microphone stand and started low. "They cut the night bus, so we walk. / They cut the library hours, so we wait. / One day this whole grey city will burn / with everything we were never allowed to say." The last line came out as a shout, and the room erupted in snaps. Pablo, who had come to support her, clapped too, but a little slower. On the walk home he kept glancing at her. Finally he asked, "The burning part. That's... a picture, right? You're not planning anything?" Leila stared at him, then burst out laughing. "Pablo! It's a metaphor. The burning is us getting loud. I'm going to the council meeting on Thursday with a petition about the bus." He grinned, embarrassed. "Okay. Good. Sorry. It was just very convincing." "That's the job," she said, and bumped him with her bag.

qa.q: What did Leila's poem say was cut?
qa.a: The night bus and the library hours were cut.

qa.q: What was Leila feeling when the last line came out as a shout?
qa.a: Leila was likely angry and frustrated about the cuts, and also exhilarated by performing; the shout was persona and exaggeration, not a real plan.

qa.q: Why was asking Leila better than deciding what the line meant?
qa.a: Lyrics use persona and exaggeration, so asking let Leila explain the metaphor and the real plan, a petition at Thursday's council meeting.

qa.q: What was it like for Pablo to hear the burning line?
qa.a: Pablo was uneasy and a little worried, clapping more slowly and asking on the walk home, then relieved and embarrassed when she explained.

grounding: It shows a teenager's slam poem using persona and exaggeration about injustice, and a listener asking before assuming the words describe real plans.

passage:
"You've been in here every lunch for three weeks, Binita."
"Is that not allowed, Ma'am?"
"It's allowed. I like the company." Zeenat Ma'am pulled up a stool. "Can I see, or is this one private?"
Binita hesitated, then turned the sketchbook around. Page after page of storm clouds, a small figure under each, getting smaller.
"These are strong," Zeenat Ma'am said. "The clouds especially. How do you feel after you draw them?"
"Lighter. For a bit. Like it's out of my head and on the paper."
"That's what art can do. I'm glad you have it." A pause. "I've also noticed you're not eating with anyone, and the person in the drawings keeps shrinking. I'm not judging the drawings. I'm asking about you. How are things, really?"
Binita picked at the spiral. "Home's loud. My parents fight a lot. I don't want to see the counsellor."
"You don't have to decide that now. Can we talk after school today, just us? Your sketchbook can come too."
"...Okay."

qa.q: What did Binita draw on every page?
qa.a: Binita drew storm clouds, with a small figure under each, getting smaller.

qa.q: How does Binita feel after drawing?
qa.a: Binita feels lighter for a bit, as if the heaviness is out of her head and on the paper; the shrinking figure also hints at sadness and loneliness about home.

qa.q: How did Zeenat Ma'am open the conversation without judging?
qa.a: She asked to see, praised the work, asked how drawing felt, then gently named what she had noticed, asked about Binita rather than the drawings, and offered a talk that same day.

qa.q: How might Zeenat Ma'am have seen three weeks of lunches in the art room?
qa.a: She likely saw it as withdrawal worth gently checking on, not something to punish, which is why she said she liked the company first.

grounding: It shows a teenager using drawing to ease stress and sadness, and an adult responding to dark themes and withdrawal with a caring conversation rather than judgement.
